Second woman dies after Friday crash near Libertyville

From the article:

Two women have died after a Friday morning crash at Milwaukee Avenue and Casey Road in an unincorporated area near Libertyville, according to Christopher Covelli, a Lake County sheriff's office spokesman.

Dawn M. Eyler, 34, of the 27400 block of 93rd Street in Salem, Wis., and Alexis J. Thompson, 22, of the 4100 block of 6th Avenue in Kenosha, Wis., were pronounced dead by officials at Advocate Condell Hospital, Covelli said.

Witnesses told police that a Chevrolet Blazer was traveling south on Milwaukee Avenue when it clipped the back of a Jeep Grand Cherokee, Covelli said. The Blazer then swerved into oncoming traffic and hit a Chevrolet Silverado that was traveling north on Milwaukee Avenue, Covelli said.

The Grand Cherokee was intending to make a right turn onto Casey Road when the Blazer made contact, Covelli said.

Investigators are still trying to determine if excessive speed played a role in the crash, Covelli said.

I drink Soylent and I love it. It has a mild taste and has all af the nutrition a person needs, including fiber. It's one calorie per milliliter, so it's very easy to count calories with it. Why did you pick 1500 calories? If you picked it because three-fourths of 2000 is a nice round number, I'd recommend you reevaluate. Look for a few online calculators that estimate your metabolism based on your weight and activity level and average the results from the different calculators. I'd recommend starting with a calorie deficit of about 400 calories per day to start with and I wouldn't even worry about exercise until you've established that you can maintain your diet as a pretty much permanent lifestyle change. If you do exercise, I'd add maybe half of what you're burning in additional calories. Diet is way more important than exercise, so you just want to make sure to not quit your diet because exercising isn't working out. With a 400 calorie deficit, you'll be able to notice your weight loss over not too long stretches of time, which for me helps maintain my motivation. Body weight naturally fluctuates, and things like water retention and how much food you have in your digestive system can temporarily skew your results, but with a calorie deficit of about 400 calories per day, your weight loss will be fairly easy notice as you track it. When I have maintained that size of a deficit, I usually reached a new lowest weight about twice a week while weighing myself everyday. A 400 calorie deficit per day will help you lose almost a pound per week. That may not be as fast as you'd like, but you're going to risk negative health consequences if you lose weight too quickly. Remember that it has taken years to accumulate your excess weight, so try to be understanding of the reality that even if you lose weight faster than you gained it, it may take a significant amount of time to get to an ideal body fat percentage.

1500 well-chosen calories per day will NOT leave you hungry and will most likely lead to a weight loss of 2lbs per week for a few months. This weight loss will slow over time. That's normal and healthy. Just keep eating your 1500 calories, and you will become the body you're eating for! :)

Also, most people lose a ridiculous amount at some point in the first month. This has to do with water and food in your stomach. Don't be discouraged if you see a 5lbs drop one week and a 1lbs drop the next. Everything evens out. I "gained" a pound 2 days ago and then "dropped" 1.5lbs overnight. It's about averages and trends. You should weigh yourself every morning naked after peeing and then record it to watch the weight bounce around but slowly decrease. :)

To be perfectly metabolically healthy, your chances are best with a BMI around 22. This is according to EXTENSIVE Harvard research. If you've never been slim, you'll have freak outs about your body looking like someone else's as you progress. Doctors will tell you to "just loose 5% (or 10%) of your weight" because they have already written you off as being a sick failure for the rest of your life, and this is the best that they hope for you. The brutal fact is, though, that weights you think are "normal" are almost certainly associated with REALLY high morbidity rates for disease. Normal, healthy-body-fat women can ALWAYS see the bones in their hands and the tops of their feet. Their knees are well-defined. Their ankles are well-defined. They have visible ribs. Not ribs that are visible where muscle or boob should be! But ribs that are visible on the lower sides of their body and above their breasts. When they lie down, their pelvic bone sticks up on the sides more than their stomachs. When they walk, their legs don't touch. They CAN touch their legs together standing if they choose to. And they can't see the outline of the pelvis all the way around. But a "healthy weight" is going to be far, far slimmer than what you've used to seeing probably in the people around you because fat people have fat friends, almost always.

Watch your blood glucose and your blood pressure and all your other health markers go into a healthy range you didn't think possible. Resting heart rate--50s or 60s. All your inflammation factors will plummet. If you can get the doctor to do it, I really encourage you to get a REALLY full blood workup to see the amazing difference that it makes. And you will be just SHOCKED at how much better you move and feel. Right now, can you run up four flights of stairs without even thinking about it, at a light, easy jog? HEALTHY PEOPLE CAN. Can you stand up from the floor without using your hands? Healthy people do that, too! That's actually a really accurate risk measure for death: http://www.dailymail.co.uk/sciencetech/article-2858804/Can-exercise-test-predict-DEATH-People-struggle-sitting-rising-test-five-times-likely-die.html

DON'T SETTLE. It's always the people who settle, with modest goals, who fail. You have ONE BODY and ONE LIFE. Why choose to have one that's slightly less shitty than it was turning out to be when you could have one that is GREAT?

I'm here because I have fat friends I really care about, and I'm tired of seeing all kinds of terrible things happen to them because of their weight. Legs lost to blood clots (caused by visceral fat, which increases clotting)--I know TWO people this happened to!!! Toes lost to diabetes. Sleep apnea that is LIFE threatening. And they have lives that are so limited. The kinds of things I do for fun, I can't even invite them along to because they can't physically do it! When I do things with them, it's going to a restaurant to eat, almost always. Or watching a show and eating. It's sooooo sad that this is all that their life can handle, while we're casually trekking miles to museums and doing canoing and paddle boats and hiking and visiting fairs and cultural exhibits. I've tried inviting them, and they just can't keep up. They end up sitting in the shade...or at a cafe. It's just painful.

Anyway, you are going to have to give up some aspects of something that's a huge part of your life RIGHT NOW, but it's a tiny part of what life has to offer. DO IT. You will be amazed that you ever let yourself live like that!

Good for you! It's so heartening to read your post; I mean clearly you have some challenges but you also are being realistic about what needs to be done and are making a plan.

I'm sorry but I have no comment on whether or not your goal for A1C level is overly optimistic. However you may want to take a look at a low carb/ketogenic diet especially if you're diabetic or leaning that way. I can make further suggestions for reading and videos if you're interested, feel free to ask. Low carb is especially helpful if you struggle with sugar cravings; you literally go from can't get enough sugar to being repulsed by sweetness.

Kudos for including exercise in your plan. Exercise is not as effective as portion control or calorie counting for weight loss though so I recommend to not make it the focus of your new lifestyle right off the bat. In the long run though being in shape -- in both senses of the word -- pays off in spades of course. If shin splints continue to be a problem then you may want to consider a 'bare foot running' style of shoe. But as I said get your diet sorted first then concentrate on getting in shape.

Everybody has advice and recommendations for things that worked, or didn't work, for them. All you can do is try stuff until you find the right combination for yourself, so keep an open in mind and prepare to make a few mistakes. You don't need to spend a pile of money on special food or a gym membership though because the real change has to come from within yourself (can't believe how cliche that sounds when i write it but it happens to be true). You can get just as good of a cardio workout in your living room. And once you stop buying prepared meals and junk food your grocery bill will drop significantly so there's no question that you'll be able to afford fresh veggies and meat.

All the best and good luck. Some days will be better than others; just keep your eye on the prize.
Thank you! I'm open to learning more about keto, so any links you can share would be awesome.

Happy to hear it. My favorite place for keto information and help is r/keto Don't let that it's reddit put you off, despite the general deterioration of the site numerous subs are still well moderated and informative (I'm in IT and I use various hardware subs all the time). There are links to many good resources along the right side, in particular the FAQ here https://www.reddit.com/r/keto/wiki/faq

There's a TONNE of information and science on keto and if you dive right in you'll probably be overwhelmed, but there's no need. You're aiming to get about 70% of your daily calories from fats and 30% from protein, a small amount of carbs are allowed but were talking like 10g/day. To start off it's about as simple as that. And as the FAQ says if in doubt increase fats and decrease carbs.

To be clear I'm not saying don't educate yourself, but I am saying do the 70/30 thing to start and then as you have questions start filling in the blanks. Keto is not recommended for certain individuals so you may want to check with your doctor. Unfortunately not all medical professionals are open to new ideas so it depends on the individual doctor BUT as always keep in mind they are trained professions and The Internet is for the most part not. Also keep in mind that you can hurt yourself if you don't pay attention. People have ended up in the hospital when they attempt keto by cutting carbs and increasing protein; weight lifters do this apparently, big mistake. Fortunately US labeling laws make it easy to check the amount of fat/protein/carb in packaged foods, and for the rest there's google.

And of course you want to be eating good fats; no trans fats/hydrogenated oils and palm oils. Coconut oil is the best all around fat in my opinion and Costco carries the big tubs for around $30 (Canada) which is a deal. Stop buying lean cuts of meat and use whole milk or cream instead of skim. After years of being taught that fats are bad this can be disconcerting at first, but if you need reassurance google current research on the link between saturated fats and heart disease (hint there isn't). And if you're a coffee fan be sure to check out recipes for Bulletproof Coffee

You'll hear about the Keto Flu and it's a real thing unfortunately. You feel like crap for a few days to a week and wonder why you're putting yourself through this, but then you start to feel better and you never look back.

You'll also hear mention of Ketosticks for testing your urine to see if you're in ketosis or not. I never found them necessary as it's quite pronounced when I go into ketosis, but everyone is different. My point here is don't necessarily buy them right off the bat but rather wait and see if you need them. Not to mention they have a rather short shelf life once opened so you either use them all or throw them away in a few months.

First things first, you are going to be making a lot of changes in your day-to-day life and so it's important to know what helps you to form a new habit. Most people, as they get older, form fewer and fewer habits and you're probably out of practice. So there's two things to know that may help you in a big way. One - it takes about three weeks of doing something on a daily basis before it starts feeling natural or automatic. Two - having a visual reminder can be a big help - like a calendar that hangs on the fridge or by your bedroom door. Cross off each day you follow your new regimen successfully and DON'T BREAK THE CHAIN.

Eating meat and vegetables is MORE IMPMORTANT than portion size so don't worry about that yet - just make sure you avoid those starches and sugars - I repeat, do not worry about your caloric intake at first. A good heuristic to follow is to avoid PROCESSED foods - for example, oil and vinegar is good on a salad but avoid caesar or thousand island dressings (and croutons are right out!). So some fruit for breakfast is OK, but avoid the jelly or jam. Sit down and PLAN OUT 3 weeks worth of meals and make your first trip to the grocery store.

Prepare yourself for TERRIBLE cravings for sugar as the yeasts in your body get desperate for their favorite food source. Do not give in.

DO NOT CONSUME ARTIFICIAL SWEETENERS. They are essentially neurotoxins and you will feel a lot better if you avoid them.

Exercise is also important, but here you have to go a bit slower. I would recommend making a habit out of going on a walk for 15 minutes in the morning and at night, either before or after your first / last meal of the day. Do this for the same 3 weeks as your dietary changes. For the shin splints, just do some stretches for 5 minutes before and after you go - get used to always doing stretches before and after your exercise.

For the love of god, get some proper exercise clothes and shoes. Nothing sucks worse than not wanting to get exercise because you don't have the proper equipment.

Set a reminder on your phone or whatever to come back here to update us on your progress. But if you don't, just increase your walking time until you're at 30 minutes twice a day - that may be 9 weeks or more away. Once you've got the basic stamina for those times, then you can think about going to the gym - say twice a week. You really want to hit the circuit machines - maybe join Planet Fitness and do the 30-minute workout they have an area set aside for.

The good news is that most people diagnosed with some type of mental illness do better once they've changed their diet and start getting exercise versus pure medication. Chances are good you'll be one of them.

You're 5'2" and not very active. I'd lower that to 1400 calories, and then you should be losing 2lbs a week across the first 6 weeks. If not, you're measuring wrong. At your height, 1400 cal is MAINTENANCE for a sedentary person of a healthy body weight.

Do not bring into the house anything you're not planning to eat. I repeat, DO NOT bring into the house anything you're not planning to eat.

Activity can make a difference of up to 50lbs. MAX. The rest is diet. You gained weight because you ate too many calories. That doesn't mean that you ate too much IN VOLUME, though you probably did a bit of that, too. But you definitely ate too much in calorie density. I can sit down and casually polish of 3000 calories in some foods without even thinking twice...for a single meal! Just about anyone can. The key to your weight loss will be:

1) Eliminate bad-habit eating. This is thoughtless, reflexive grazing when you're not hungry.

2) Divorce yourself from the emotions of eating. You're not a dog. Don't reward yourself with food. Don't comfort yourself with food. A lot of our lives end up being marked by food in some way. "I feel bad, so I'm going to wrap up, watch movies, and eat junk." "I finished that big project, so I'm going to celebrate with a great dinner!" "I did a GREAT job dieting all week, so I deserve this!" Noooooooooooo. Find other things to reward yourself with. Get your nails done. Get your hair done. Set up your clothes or jewelry shopping to make it your reward. Go to the beach. Watch the sunset. Zero-calorie rewards from here on out.

3) You're going to have to de-socialize your eating. If you've got fat friends, everything you do probably revolves around food. Come over for movies...and food. Go out with the girls...and eat. Have a party...and order out. You can a) budget for this in your calories (as a slim girl who was briefly overweight, my ordinary strategy was usually to skip a meal or two to account for these calorie-fests--it was automatic, not conscious, and my fat friends always said, "I don't know how you stay skinny!" Um, because I didn't have breakfast or lunch, and you had both, and now you're going to go home and have a snack for bed....). Or you can b) just eat less. Most people end up combining the two. You can try to get your friends to be less food-focused, but if they don't want change, they won't be receptive.

4) You're going to have to ACCURATELY count your calories and figure out a new eating pattern of things you like that fill you us. I got chubby due to inactivity plus getting into bad habits with calorie dense foods. I had to pay VERY close attention to calorie counts to discover my "problem areas" and then to rearrange my habits in a healthier pattern. DIETITIANS CAN'T ESTIMATE CALORIES CORRECTLY. No one can. After a year or more of eating well, you'll be in a good "groove", but it will be your habits carrying you along. To develop proper habits, you must weigh everything you eat down to the GRAM. 2x per week, you can do some social eating and estimate, based on the online menu counters, how many calories things have, but more than that can throw off your counts considerably.

YOU DON'T HAVE TO EAT YUCKY FOOD FOR THE REST OF YOUR LIFE. This is a deep fear of many obese people because they are so emotionally attached to their food and eating. But frankly...most obese people don't get obese eating food that's actually delicious. There are foods that hit the palatability button on a lot of people but aren't actually GOOD. The BMIs of the adults in my family are 19(me, female, body fat percent 20% and falling as I get back into shape) and 22(husband, dancer and weightlifter, body fat percent 10% and stable for more than 15 years). My kids' BMIs are in the 15th to 25th percentile. For us, this is a typical week:

*- Indian curry from scratch

  • -Middle eastern butternut squash dish

  • -Spaghetti squash with tomatoes and olives drizzled with olive oil

  • -Sweet potatoes

  • -Moroccan chickpea dish

  • -A couple of salmon filets to round out otherwise vegetarian fare

  • -Chinese gai lan

  • -Chinese beef with broccoli and mushrooms

  • -Side-salads with nuts and dried fruit, maybe a homemade dressing

  • -Enchilada soup

  • -Berries in yogurt sweetened with Stevia

  • -Whole-grain cereal (I'm a breakfast cereal girl! Easy and fast, and I dont' always feel like oatmeal)

  • -Oatmeal with dried fruit

Maybe these aren't your things, but they're restaurant-quality meals that have a lot fewer calories per serving. We eat out once a week, too, by the way, at a GOOD restaurant.

For your health, these are the order that things go in:

  • 1) Healthy body fat percentage and fat free mass index

  • 2) Not smoking

*3) Exercise and nutrition

Body fat and fat free mass are tied because below a certain amount of fat free mass, like in very elderly immobile people and anorexics, FFM becomes more important that BF. For everyone else, BF is more important.

Not smoking is obvious.

Exercise and nutrition are tied. People who are very lean who have good nutrition but don't exercise have better biomarkers for many illnesses than people who do exercise and are less attentive to nutrition. (The studies of calorie restriction with optimal nutrition bears this out.) But without exercise even with great nutrition, you're more likely to get dementia and osteoporosis and much less likely to survive cancer and other illnesses.

But those are your priorities for health. Body fat percentage and muscle FIRST, nutrition and exercise SECOND (presuming you don't smoke).

That said.....

You should aim to walk 5 miles a day just through the course of your daily life. shin splints are going to be a problem now. Bind them up in the morning and be gentle. If you push yourself to injury, that's sabotage. Stop when it hurts, but try to average 10% more steps every week using a FitBit or pedometer app until you're at 10,000. This isn't exercise. It gets you into the the "normally sedentary" zone only.

As you lose weight and get more mobile, start with lifting weights. Just 2x per week, 30-45min each time. That's seriously all you need to get 90% of the benefit. Schedule it into your calendar. You need to be able to move your arms and legs correctly through the range of motion of the exercises to do this. I don't know what weight that is for you. If you can do it now, start now.

I don't recommend swimming. It's easy to lazily glide about and think you're working out when you're not. When you can, biking is good, and running is frankly BETTER. The impact of the running makes the padding in the joints thicker and prevents arthritis. You just have to be light and strong enough that you can run without immediately injuring yourself. That's what the walking, weights, and weightloss help with. Start by running for :30 and walking for 1:30. Gradually increase the running by :05 until you're running :60 and walking 1:30. Then lower your walking intervals until you're walking :30. Then raise your running interval as you can. :) Do this for an hour 3x a week at first, but as you get faster, you can shorten your distance. Eventually, you should be able to do a few miles without walking. If you run 3x per week, 4-6 miles each time, and at a moderate pace, you'll get your recommended 2h30min of aerobic exercise in. I like the idea of Couch to 5k, but I think it pushes a lot of people way too hard...and then sets a low bar for the long term. This is ON TOP of your 10k steps a day.

  • 218lbs--no longer morbidly obese!

PEOPLE WITH AMBITIOUS GOALS LOSE MORE WEIGHT. Forget "realistic goals." You'll be rocking a size 6 while all those people with "realistic goals" have gained all their weight back and more. Fight for the body that YOU want.

Now you can start tracking your waist and body fat percentage.

  • Professionally measured DEXA/bodpod/displacement BF% of 35% or below--no longer obese according to BF%!

At the same time:

  • Waist circumference <35" measured at top of belly button--out of highest category for visceral fat!
  • <32" at top of belly button--out of high risk category for visceral fat!
  • <28" at top of belly button--in low risk category for for visceral fat!
